_comment: Key lessons, seeded from docs/doctrine.md rather than written fresh. Each lesson points at real assets already on the map so it can be demonstrated rather than just asserted — clicking one frames those assets in the 3D view. `doctrine_ref` names the section of doctrine.md the claim comes from; `source_tag` uses the sourcing key at the bottom of that file. Adding a lesson is adding an entry here — no code change.

lessons.title: The kill chain collapsed from hours to minutes
lessons.summary: Find, decide and strike used to take hours through a chain of people. It is now routinely single-digit minutes.
lessons.detail: Traditional call-for-fire moved through observers, staff checks, airspace deconfliction and commander approval — hours. Here a reconnaissance drone finds a target, artillery responds in under a minute once a firing solution exists, and an FPV finishes anything needing precision. The honest caveat, from a former Ukrainian FPV operator: strikes still sometimes take 30+ minutes, and the time is lost to deconfliction overhead rather than to jamming — so treat 'minutes' as the achievable case, not the uniform one.

lessons.title: Drones cause 60–70% of equipment losses
lessons.summary: Not artillery, not direct fire. The cheapest system on the battlefield is destroying the most expensive ones.
lessons.detail: 60–70% of equipment losses on both sides are now attributed to drones. Put next to unit cost, that is the procurement argument in one line: a loitering munition costing tens of thousands routinely removes armour costing millions. Compare the cost tiles on a strike UAV and a main battle tank directly — both are on the map, and the ratio is the lesson.

lessons.title: Control of the lower sky sets how close you can stand
lessons.summary: Disposition depth is decided by local drone superiority, not by doctrine or preference.
lessons.detail: The single sharpest finding in the reference material. The side holding control of the lower sky can deploy 1–1.5 km from the line and use direct-fire tank positions. The side without it is pushed back to roughly 7 km and restricted to indirect fire. Everything else about depth on this map — where the artillery sits, where the command posts sit, where casualties are collected — follows from which side that is on a given day.

lessons.title: Detection is a multi-day pattern, not an event
lessons.summary: Nobody finds a drone team with one sighting. They follow the drone home and watch for days.
lessons.detail: The method both sides use is the same: don't engage the returning drone, follow it. Watch the landing point, note the resupply vehicle, look for a repeating daily flight path. A battalion sector's drone positions get substantially mapped in 2–7 days this way. The defensive consequence is what matters here — camouflage discipline and route variation are what stop a unit being mapped the same way, and antenna losses are disproportionately costly because spares aren't stocked forward.

lessons.title: EW is the invisible battlefield everything else depends on
lessons.summary: Sensors, drones and comms only work if the electromagnetic fight is being won.
lessons.detail: Passive RF triangulation (5–20 m accuracy), active radar, soft-kill jamming and hard-kill interceptors stack into a layered fight that decides whether anything else on this map functions. The counter-intuitive part is organisational rather than technical: procurement is often decentralised, units buy their own jammers, and the resulting uncoordinated 'unofficial EW fields' degrade friendly drone performance as much as enemy drones.

lessons.title: Fibre-optic control links took jamming off the table
lessons.summary: A spool of glass defeats the entire soft-kill EW layer, at the cost of manoeuvre.
lessons.detail: A wired FPV trails a fibre-optic control link and is simply immune to RF jamming — the dominant countermeasure stops applying. The trade is real (reduced manoeuvrability, a finite spool), but it is why the strike envelope on the ruler carries two separate sourced markers: a radio-FPV envelope and a wider fibre-optic one. It is also the clearest example on this map of a cheap change to one system invalidating an expensive investment in another.

lessons.title: Kill chains pushed down to squad level
lessons.summary: Infantry increasingly find, decide and strike with their own drones instead of requesting fires from above.
lessons.detail: The authority to complete a kill chain has moved down rather than concentrating at higher HQ. A squad with organic drones is no longer only a consumer of supporting fires — it is a full sensor-to-shooter loop on its own. That reshapes the C2 graph on this map: the dependency edges that used to run up and back down an echelon now increasingly close locally.
lessons.source_tag: [web: Small Wars Journal — Distributed Combat Power]

lessons.title: The deep rear stopped being a sanctuary
lessons.summary: Cheap one-way systems reach targets thousands of kilometres behind the line.
lessons.detail: Depth used to buy safety: past a few hundred kilometres, an asset was effectively out of reach of anything but strategic systems. Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb reached airfields roughly 4,300 km from the front using smuggled short-range drones launched locally. The consequence for this map is that the deepest band is no longer a rear area in the traditional sense — power generation, logistics hubs and airfields are all now inside somebody's reach.

lessons.title: Consumption rates, not inventories, decide sustainment
lessons.summary: A single FPV company can burn through ~7,200 munitions a month. Heavy multirotors survive 5–10 missions.
lessons.detail: Illustrative unit economics (a Lithuanian projection grounded in Ukrainian usage rates, not Ukrainian actuals): one FPV company at intensive tempo consumes roughly 7,200 kamikaze drones per month, and a heavy 'Baba Yaga'-type multirotor typically survives only 5–10 missions before loss. Planning against an inventory number rather than a monthly burn rate is how a drone programme runs dry in its second month.

lessons.title: A ~30 km drone-dense corridor either side of the line
lessons.summary: Persistent drone coverage genuinely dominates a band about 30 km deep on both sides of a ~1,200 km front.
lessons.detail: This is the band where movement in daylight is a decision rather than a routine, and it is why so much of the disposition on this map clusters just outside it. Russian offensive staging sits up to 30 km back with movement to the line split into guided segments over 3–4 days under radio silence and paper orders; FPV launch teams sit 8–10 km back with their control and relay equipment a further ~10 km behind that.
